To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Nb-Y-Zr diagram is a useful discriminant for distinguishing melts derived from depleted mantle, from those derived from the deep mantle.

(i) Nb/Y and Zr/Y ratios can be used as a simple discriminant to distinguish hot spot and arc-related components in mafic rocks; (ii) the Nb/Y-Zr/Y plot can be used to identify a hot spot component in mafics from continental flood basalts and oceanic plateaus, and to show that the Bunbury Basalts, Australia, and some Rajmahal lavas, India, were derived from a plume source; (iii

the Nb-Y-Zr diagram is a useful tool for identifying deep-mantle components in mafic volcanic rocks, and that the Reunion and Kerguelen hot spots were active in the Late Cretaceous and Cenozoic, and in the Jurassic, respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the origin of continental flood basalts, and the relationship between plume-related and plate tectonic processes.
the study of the geochemistry of the mantle and crust, the origin of the continental crust and the nature of the deep continental roots.
the origin and evolution of the Earth's crust and upper mantle, the processes of continental and oceanic crustal formation, and the nature and evolution of the deep Earth.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence for a hot spot signature in the Bunbury Basin.

the Reunion plume has been a major component in the Deccans, but not in the Rajmahal, whereas the Kerguelan plume has been an important component of the Deccan, Rajmahal, and Bunbury Basalts, but not of the Ninetyeast Ridge.
the Reunion plume is the source of the Deccan traps, and that the Kerguelan plume is the cause of the Kergue- len plateau, but not of the Rajmahal Traps.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the mantle source regions of the Deccan Trap lavas are a mixture of the Kergu- elen plume, the Reunion plume, the subcontinental lithosphere and, in some cases, the subcontinental crust.
there are two types of mantle source for flood basalt magmatism: a depleted component and an enriched component, the latter derived from a deep-mantled plume source.
the deep-mantle source component is not as common or as important as once thought.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Nb-Y-Zr relationship can help to distinguish the deep-mantle signature from the signature of arc-related crustal contamination in mafic magmas.
the mantle source region of the Bunbury Basalts, and by extension the Kerguelan plume, has been depleted of Nb, Y, and Zr, relative to the Reunion plume source.
the deep-mantle plumes are more widespread than previously thought.
